analysis.investment_thesis: Wakefit has a recognizable D2C brand with 25% revenue CAGR (₹797→₹1,256 Cr), but persistent net losses in all three years — including a widening ₹35 Cr loss in FY25 vs ₹15 Cr in FY24 — make PEG analysis impossible and violate my core GARP discipline. At EV/EBITDA of 54.9x for a company that can't convert EBITDA to net profit, the market is pricing in perfection the company hasn't earned yet.
key_strengths: Revenue compounding at ~25% CAGR over 3 years — the growth story is real
Gross margin of 54.17% signals genuine brand pricing power in a commodity-adjacent category
Operating CF turned positive and held: ₹81 Cr in FY24 and ₹77 Cr in FY25 — cash engine improving
key_risks: No path to net profit visible — losses widened from ₹15 Cr (FY24) to ₹35 Cr (FY25) despite EBITDA improving to ₹83 Cr; finance costs nearly doubled to ₹30 Cr
Debt surging from ₹144 Cr to ₹273 Cr while cash evaporated from ₹62 Cr to ₹7 Cr — balance sheet stress accelerating
FCF declining (₹52 Cr → ₹26 Cr) while capex jumped to ₹51 Cr, suggesting the growth machine requires more feed to sustain momentum
red_flags: PEG ratio is incalculable — earnings are negative; this is the one metric I need most
P/E of 118x on a loss-making company signals the market is using adjusted/fictional earnings
Net losses worsened in FY25 after nearly breaking even in FY24 — the story is going backward on the bottom line
Promoter holding at only 37% for a founder-driven D2C brand is low — raises questions about conviction
analysis.detailed_analysis:
I love a story I can walk into a store and understand — Wakefit sells mattresses and furniture online, revenue growing 25%+ annually, and the gross margin at 54% tells me customers will pay a premium for the brand. That's the kind of business I'd notice. But here's the problem: I need earnings. Peter Lynch doesn't buy hope, he buys growth at a reasonable price, and you can't compute a PEG ratio on negative earnings. Net losses in all three years, widening to ₹35 Cr in FY25 despite EBITDA reaching ₹83 Cr — that gap is being eaten by finance costs (up to ₹30 Cr) and D&A. The operating income line swung from +₹2 Cr in FY24 back to -₹5 Cr in FY25. That's not a trend, that's a wobble.

The balance sheet story is equally troubling. Debt jumped from ₹144 Cr to ₹273 Cr in two years while cash fell from ₹62 Cr to ₹7 Cr. Equity is actually shrinking — ₹544 Cr in FY24 to ₹521 Cr in FY25 — as losses eat into capital. At ₹4,905 Cr market cap on ₹1,256 Cr revenue and no profits, the market is asking me to pay 3.4x sales and 55x EBITDA for a company that can't get out of the red. I've seen this movie before with hot D2C IPOs — the story sounds great but the numbers don't add up. Pass until they show two consecutive years of real net profit.
